title: Starting from where you are
examples: I want to exercise but cannot get started.
Make the first action tiny: put on comfortable shoes or clear a little space. You can decide the rest afterwards.
I have not exercised in a long time.
Start gently and build gradually. If you have health concerns or have been inactive for a long time, check with a clinician first.
I feel embarrassed being a beginner.
Beginning is a place to start, not something to hide. Choose a movement you can learn at a comfortable pace.
I need an exercise plan that is not intimidating.
Try one of the gentle routines in Move. Read the first step before deciding whether it fits today.
I am waiting until I feel motivated.
You could try the smallest practical beginning before motivation arrives. Opening the routine can be that beginning.
I bought exercise clothes but have not used them.
The clothes can wait without becoming a judgment. Choose one short, comfortable activity you actually want to try.
I want to feel stronger but do not know where to begin.
Look at First steps strength in Move. Start within your comfort and get qualified guidance if the movements are unfamiliar.
Can getting ready count as progress?
It can make the next step easier. Notice the preparation, then choose whether a little movement fits right now.
I need permission to start very small.
You can start smaller than the plan in your head. A manageable beginning is easier to return to.
What if I stop after one exercise?
Then you did one exercise. You can learn from how it felt without treating a shorter session as failure.

title: Movement in a small gap
examples: I only have five minutes to move.
Five minutes can be a real opportunity. The Desk break routine offers a simple place to start.
Is ten minutes even worth doing?
A short session is still movement. Choose something that fits the time you actually have.
I cannot fit a full workout into today.
You can choose a smaller version or a short walk. The day does not need an all-or-nothing decision.
I have a break while dinner cooks.
Keep an eye on the cooking and choose something safe nearby. Do not leave a hot stove unattended to exercise.
I have fifteen minutes between appointments.
Choose a routine that leaves time to settle afterwards. The gap does not need to be filled to its last second.
Can I split movement across the day?
You can use smaller opportunities when they fit. Notice what is practical, rather than waiting for one perfect long session.
I want to move before a call starts.
Pick a gentle activity with a clear ending. Leave yourself a little time to become comfortable for the call.
I keep cancelling because the workout is too long.
Make the planned session shorter before the next attempt. A plan that fits your life is easier to use.
I have two minutes and need a change of position.
If comfortable, stand or shift position and move gently. Keep the movement suited to your body and surroundings.
I did half my planned walk.
Half a walk still happened. Record what you actually did, if you want, and leave out the punishment for the rest.

title: A break from the desk
examples: I have been at my desk for hours.
If you can, take a short movement break now. Change position and choose a comfortable way to move.
My shoulders feel tense from working.
Try an easier position and a gentle movement within comfort. Do not force a stretch or push into pain.
I want a desk break that will not make me sweaty.
Choose a gentle routine or a short easy walk. A break does not need to become a workout.
I cannot leave my desk for long.
A brief change of position may still fit. Keep it safe and comfortable within the space you have.
Can I move while a file is downloading?
That can be a useful cue. If it is practical, step away for a comfortable movement while you wait.
I keep forgetting to get up.
Link a movement pause to something you already notice, like finishing a call. A reliable device reminder is another option.
I need a seated movement option.
Choose a supported position and movements already comfortable for you. For tailored seated exercises, ask a qualified professional.
I feel stiff after concentrating for a long time.
Start with a gentle change of position. Give yourself room to move without trying to undo the whole day at once.
Can I stretch through the pain in my neck?
Do not push through pain. Stop the movement and seek appropriate professional advice if the pain persists or concerns you.
live
I want to come back to work after a short walk.
Before leaving, note the next task step. That can make returning easier after your movement break.

title: Make a walk easier to choose
examples: I want to go for a walk but keep postponing it.
Choose a simple route and put on your shoes. You do not need to decide on a perfect distance first.
I do not know where to walk.
Pick somewhere familiar and safe for your circumstances. A short route you already know can reduce the decisions.
I want a walk without tracking steps.
You can walk without a number. Choose the route or time that suits you and let the movement be enough.
I feel awkward walking alone.
A familiar, comfortable route may make the start easier. You can also invite someone, without waiting for company every time.
Can I walk slowly?
Yes. Choose a pace that fits your comfort and situation. A walk does not have to become a competition.
I want a little walk after lunch.
If it suits you, choose a comfortable route and pace. The After-meal stroll routine can keep the plan simple.
I do not want to turn a walk into exercise homework.
Then leave the targets out. You can notice the surroundings and return when it feels practical.
I walked to the shop instead of doing a workout.
That was still movement in your day. You can record it without pretending it was a different kind of session.
I am worried about getting distracted near traffic.
Keep your attention on the route and surroundings. Leave the screen and any inward-focus exercise until you are safely stopped.
Can you choose a walking route near me?
I do not have a verified local route here. Use a trusted map and check the route's suitability for your circumstances.
live

title: When the weather changes the plan
examples: It is raining and I do not want to walk.
You can choose an indoor alternative or a shorter plan. Weather changing the activity does not erase your intention.
It is too hot for my usual workout.
Adjust or postpone the session if conditions are uncomfortable. A gentler indoor option may fit better than forcing the original plan.
The pavement is icy.
Choose a safer option rather than keeping the walk at any cost. An indoor movement break may be enough today.
It is dark before I finish work.
Consider a well-lit familiar route, a different time, or an indoor activity. Your comfort and safety matter more than the exact plan.
I cannot open the windows because of the weather.
Choose an activity that feels comfortable in the room you have. You can reduce the intensity or take a rest instead.
I planned a run but conditions look unsafe.
It is reasonable to change the plan. Pick another activity or wait for safer conditions.
I need movement for a rainy weekend.
Look through the no-equipment routines in Move. Choose one that suits your space and current ability.
I feel guilty using the weather as a reason to stay in.
You can make a practical decision without judging it. Ask whether an indoor option fits, or whether today calls for rest.
Can you check the weather before my walk?
Use a current local forecast before deciding. This recording cannot check live weather or tell you conditions are safe.
live
I want a backup plan for outdoor exercise.
Choose one indoor option in advance. A simple backup can save you from making the whole decision again on a difficult day.

title: Move in the space you have
examples: My home is too small for a workout.
Check the space needed for each movement before starting. Choose a smaller, safe option rather than forcing the routine into a cramped area.
I have downstairs neighbours and cannot jump.
Try the Quiet living-room cardio routine. Read each movement and adapt or skip anything unsuitable for your space.
I do not own any exercise equipment.
Several Move routines need no equipment. Start with one that matches your experience and the room available.
The floor is cluttered.
Clear only the safe space needed before moving. If that is not possible, choose another activity or place.
Can I use household objects as weights?
Only use equipment that is stable and suitable for the movement. If unsure, choose a no-equipment exercise or ask for qualified guidance.
I want to exercise without disturbing anyone.
Choose quiet, controlled movements and a practical time. You can keep the session gentle and short.
I cannot get down to the floor comfortably.
Skip floor-based movements. Choose an accessible alternative and seek tailored guidance if you need help finding suitable exercises.
I need a routine in my living room.
Open Move and choose No equipment or Around the house. Read the routine and check the space before beginning.
tool
My pet keeps getting under my feet.
Pause and make the area safe before continuing. You do not need to finish a set while avoiding an obstacle.
I want to move while the house is busy.
Find a safe space and choose a brief activity that fits. It is also okay to wait for a less crowded moment.

title: Make the gym less daunting
examples: I am nervous about going to the gym.
Give the first visit a small purpose, such as learning the layout. You do not have to master everything on arrival.
I do not know how to use the machines.
Ask a qualified member of staff to show you. It is better to learn the setup than guess under load.
The gym is crowded and my plan is falling apart.
You can wait, choose a suitable alternative you know, or shorten the session. The exact order is not a test.
I feel like everyone is watching me.
That feeling can be uncomfortable. Keep your attention on one familiar exercise and ask staff for support if it would help.
I want a simple full-body gym session.
The Gym full body routines give a starting structure. Get instruction for unfamiliar movements and choose loads appropriate to your experience.
I am embarrassed to ask for help at the gym.
Learning the equipment is a reasonable reason to ask. A short question can make your session clearer and safer.
I forgot my usual gym equipment.
Choose a session that works safely with what you have. You do not need to improvise a risky replacement.
I want to leave after ten minutes at the gym.
You can decide what fits today. A short visit can still help you learn what would make the next one easier.
I am comparing my weights with someone nearby.
Their training is not your instruction. Choose a load you can control with the technique you have learned.
Can you check my lifting form through this recording?
No. This recording cannot see your technique. Ask a qualified coach for feedback on the movement you are doing.
live

title: Learning strength work
examples: What do sets and reps mean?
A rep is one repetition of a movement. A set is a group of those repetitions before you rest.
What does three sets of eight mean?
It means eight repetitions, then a rest, repeated for three sets. The movement and load still need to suit you.
I want to gain strength without rushing.
Learn movements you can control, keep the effort appropriate, and build gradually. Consistency can be a gentler goal than constant increases.
Do I have to lift heavy on my first day?
No. Start with learning the movement and an appropriate level of resistance. Qualified guidance can help you choose.
I keep forgetting which set I am on.
Use a simple note or the routine's set display. You do not need to hold the whole session in memory.
Can strength training include bodyweight movements?
Yes, bodyweight movements can be part of strength work. Choose versions suitable for your current ability and comfort.
I want to build muscle but need a starting point.
Start with a manageable strength routine and regular nourishment. Personal training and nutrition advice can help tailor the plan to you.
I am confused by all the exercise terminology.
Choose one movement at a time. Learn what that movement asks of you before worrying about the rest of the vocabulary.
How do I know whether an exercise suits me?
Consider your experience, comfort and any health limits. A qualified professional can help if you are unsure about a specific movement.
Should I copy a strong person's programme?
Their programme may not fit your experience or recovery. Use your own starting point and get guidance where you need it.

title: Keep an honest movement record
examples: Log my strength session.
Open Record a strength session, then check the exercises, sets, reps and weights before saving your record.
tool
I forgot to record yesterday's walk.
You can add it with yesterday's date. Use a reasonable estimate rather than inventing exact minutes you do not remember.
tool
I used different weights in different sets.
Record the sets as accurately as the form allows. A note can preserve any detail that does not fit neatly.
I only completed some of the routine.
Save the steps you actually completed. The record is useful because it is honest, not because every box is filled.
Can I record a stretch as movement?
Yes. Give it a clear title and record the time you actually spent, if you want it in your history.
tool
I typed the wrong weight into my workout.
Edit the saved entry and review the units and numbers before saving the correction.
tool
Do I need to estimate calories burned?
No. A useful movement record can simply describe what you did and how long it took. No calorie estimate is required.
I want to see my last session for this exercise.
Look at the previous records for the same exercise. Compare like with like, including the way you performed it.
tool
My activity did not save.
Check the saved movement list before trying again, so you do not create a duplicate. If needed, keep a temporary note.
tool
Can you confirm how many workouts I did this month?
That needs your actual saved history. Open the relevant dates; this recording cannot verify a personal total.
tool

title: Build without rushing
examples: Should I increase my weights every workout?
Progress does not have to happen every session. Keep technique and recovery in view, and seek guidance on increases that suit you.
I did the same reps as last time.
Repeating a session can still be useful practice. Look at the longer pattern rather than demanding an improvement every time.
How do I know when to make an exercise harder?
When you are comfortable with the current version, ask a qualified coach about an appropriate next step. Avoid guessing through pain.
I want to add more before I have learned the basics.
Give the basics enough time. A movement you can control is a better starting point than a bigger number you cannot manage.
My strength has not changed this week.
A week may not tell you much. Look at consistency, context and comparable records over more time.
I feel stronger but the numbers are unchanged.
Notice what has become easier or more controlled. Progress is not only an increase in the weight on the record.
Can you guarantee muscle gain in a month?
I cannot guarantee a result or timeline. Training, nourishment, recovery and individual circumstances all affect what happens.
live
I am tempted to double everything tomorrow.
A sudden jump is not necessary to make progress. Choose a manageable next session and build with appropriate guidance.
I want a harder option for this movement.
Use the routine's harder option only if it fits your ability and you understand the technique. You can keep the current version.
I went backwards on one exercise.
One session can vary for many reasons. Record it honestly and look at the pattern before deciding something has gone wrong.

title: Recovery belongs in the plan
examples: I feel guilty taking a rest day.
Rest can be part of training, not a break from being committed. Let today's plan reflect how you are doing.
I am tired but do not want to lose my streak.
A streak is not more important than your wellbeing. Choose rest or a gentler option when that is what you need.
Can I have a day without tracking movement?
Yes. You can move or rest without recording it. The app does not need evidence for every choice.
I trained hard yesterday and feel drained.
Consider a lighter day or rest. You do not need to repeat yesterday's effort just to feel consistent.
I am recovering from an illness.
Return gradually and follow any medical advice you have. If symptoms persist or you are unsure, ask a healthcare professional before exercising.
I want a gentle recovery activity.
Choose a comfortable easy movement you already know, or simply rest. Recovery does not need its own demanding checklist.
I am frustrated that my body needs rest.
You can be frustrated and still respond kindly. The next useful step may be making recovery easier, not arguing with it.
I skipped today because I was exhausted.
That was a response to the day you had. Decide the next session when you know what capacity you have.
Can more exercise make up for poor recovery?
Adding effort is not a substitute for recovery. Consider your rest and overall load, and get tailored advice if you are struggling.
I want to plan rest without calling it failure.
Give rest its own place in the plan. You can describe it as recovery, or simply leave that space unfilled.

title: Listen when movement feels wrong
examples: This exercise hurts sharply.
Stop that movement. Do not push through sharp pain; seek appropriate medical advice, especially if pain is severe or persistent.
live
I feel dizzy during my workout.
Stop exercising and get somewhere safe to rest. Seek urgent help if symptoms are severe, persistent, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms.
live
I have chest pain and feel short of breath while exercising.
Stop and call emergency services now. In the UK, call nine nine nine. Do not continue the workout or wait for this app.
urgent
My knee hurts in this squat.
Stop the squat rather than forcing the range. A qualified professional can help assess the pain and suggest a suitable alternative.
live
Should I push through because the routine says so?
No. A routine is not more important than pain or feeling unwell. Stop and choose appropriate support.
I am sore after trying something new.
Keep the next activity gentle and avoid forcing painful movement. Seek professional advice if the soreness is severe, unusual or does not improve.
Can you tell whether I have pulled a muscle?
I cannot assess an injury from this recording. Stop the painful activity and seek appropriate professional advice.
live
My joint is swollen after exercise.
Avoid pushing the affected area and get medical advice. This needs assessment rather than a motivational message to continue.
live
I do not know the difference between effort and pain.
If you are unsure, stop and ask a qualified professional. You do not need to discover the limit by forcing through discomfort.
I feel unwell but want to finish the last set.
End the set and attend to how you feel. Finishing the number is not worth ignoring a possible health problem.

title: Movement that fits your body
examples: Standing exercise is not accessible to me.
Your movement plan should fit your body. Choose suitable seated or supported options with guidance from a qualified professional where needed.
I use a wheelchair and want to record activity.
You can describe the activity you actually did in your movement journal. Walking is not the only movement worth recording.
I have a disability and generic routines do not fit.
You do not need to force the generic routine. Personalised advice can help identify movements that suit your access needs and health.
I need a lower-impact version.
Check the easier option and whether it is suitable for you. You can skip the movement if neither version fits.
I cannot follow fast exercise instructions.
Read the next step before starting and pause whenever you need. The routine can wait for you.
I want to repeat the instruction before moving.
Take another look at the current step. Understanding the movement matters more than keeping up with a timer.
My energy changes a lot from day to day.
Plan for that variation. Keep a smaller option available and seek tailored advice if you have a condition affecting activity.
I need support for balance.
Choose a safe, stable setup and guidance appropriate to you. Do not attempt an unsupported movement that feels unsafe.
I cannot perform the exercise shown.
That is useful information, not a failure. Choose an appropriate alternative or skip it; the routine should adapt to you.
I want movement goals that are not about steps.
You can focus on an activity, a skill, or how manageable it feels. A step count is only one possible measure.

title: Encouragement without pressure
examples: Motivate me without shouting at me.
You do not need to attack this session. Choose one comfortable beginning, and let that be enough to get moving.
I do not want fitness guilt.
Then leave guilt out of the plan. Choose movement because it fits your needs today, not because you owe a punishment.
Can you keep me company while I exercise?
Bounce can stay with your activity in Daywell. Choose quiet company or a little encouragement in the activity settings.
tool
I want encouragement but not constant talking.
Choose A little encouragement or Stay quiet. The company can be there without interrupting every moment.
tool
I am bored of my usual workout.
You could change one part you understand safely, or choose a different routine. Variety does not need to mean starting from zero.
I am not in the mood but might try a little.
Try a small beginning and reassess. You are allowed to decide how much fits after you start.
I want to enjoy movement again.
Think of an activity you like for its own sake. Music, a familiar route, or friendly company may make the choice easier.
I need a gentler reason to exercise.
You might move to feel a little more capable in everyday life. It does not have to be about changing your appearance.
I hate being told no excuses.
Your circumstances are real. Let the plan account for them instead of treating every difficulty as something to overpower.
Say something encouraging before I start.
Start where you are today. A controlled, manageable effort is enough; you do not have to impress anyone here.

title: Company and movement
examples: I would exercise more if someone joined me.
Try one simple invitation with a specific time. A short walk can be easier to arrange than a whole new fitness plan.
My friend is much fitter than I am.
Agree on a pace and activity that work for both of you. You do not need to turn shared time into a test.
I am worried about slowing the group down.
Check the group's pace and expectations before joining. Finding a suitable group is more useful than forcing yourself to keep up.
I want to ask someone to walk with me.
Make the invitation easy to answer: Would you like a short walk after lunch one day this week?
My workout partner cancelled.
You can choose a smaller solo option or reschedule. Their cancellation does not have to decide every part of your plan.
I do not enjoy group exercise.
You can choose movement on your own terms. A solo routine is just as valid a preference.
I feel pressured to lift what my friend lifts.
Choose your own load and technique. Training together does not mean your bodies or experience need identical numbers.
I want movement time with my family.
Choose an activity everyone can take part in comfortably. The shared experience can matter more than a training target.
I am embarrassed to tell a trainer I need an easier option.
That is useful information for a trainer. Ask for a version that fits your current ability and comfort.
I want accountability without being judged.
Agree on what support you actually want, such as a friendly check-in. Make clear that rest and changed plans are allowed.

title: Movement away from your routine
examples: I am travelling and have no gym.
The no-equipment routines can give you options. Check the space and choose what feels suitable after the journey.
I have been sitting on a train for ages.
When it is safe and practical, change position or take a gentle movement break. Stay aware of the train and people around you.
I am stiff after a long drive.
Wait until you are safely parked. Then choose a comfortable change of position and gentle movement without forcing a stretch.
I want a short hotel-room routine.
Open Hotel room fifteen in Move and review the exercises. Adapt or skip anything that does not fit the room or your body.
tool
I forgot my trainers on a trip.
Choose an activity that is safe with the footwear and surroundings you have. You do not need to improvise a risky workout.
My holiday has disrupted my exercise routine.
You can let the holiday have a different rhythm. Notice ordinary movement without recreating every usual workout.
I feel drained after a long flight.
Start with rest and comfort. You can choose gentle movement when it feels appropriate, rather than forcing the usual session.
I need a movement break at a service station.
Once safely parked, choose a safe place to walk or change position. Keep clear of traffic and return when you feel ready.
I want to restart after travelling.
Use a manageable first session and see how it feels. You do not need to make up every missed activity.
Can you track my movement automatically while I travel?
This MVP does not automatically track your travel activity. You can add a movement record yourself when you want one.
tool

title: Understand before increasing effort
examples: I do not understand this exercise cue.
Pause the routine and read it again. If the movement is still unclear, get a qualified demonstration rather than guessing.
How fast should I do these repetitions?
Use a controlled pace you have learned for the exercise. Speed is not a substitute for understanding the movement.
I keep losing count while learning the movement.
Put technique first. A simple counter or note can help, but the number does not need to override control.
Can I watch a demonstration before starting?
A clear demonstration from a qualified source can help. Daywell's text cue alone may not be enough for an unfamiliar exercise.
I am holding my breath while lifting and feel uncomfortable.
Stop and reset. Ask a qualified coach about breathing and technique appropriate to that lift rather than pushing through discomfort.
The harder version looks exciting.
Understand the easier version first. Choose difficulty that matches your skill, not just the version that looks impressive.
I do not know where my feet should go.
That detail depends on the exercise and your body. Get a clear demonstration before adding resistance or speed.
Can you correct my posture from what I tell you?
I cannot reliably assess your movement from a short description. A qualified coach or clinician can observe and guide you.
live
I want to practise rather than chase a number.
That is a useful intention. Keep the effort manageable and notice whether the movement feels more controlled.
I rushed the last set and it felt messy.
Pause before continuing. You can reduce the demand and return to a version you can control, or end the session.

title: Time a little movement
examples: Start a ten-minute walk timer.
Review the proposed walk and duration before starting. Keep Daywell open if you want the timer and companion cues.
tool
Pause my workout timer.
Use Pause activity or the routine's Pause button. Check the on-screen timer to confirm it has stopped.
tool
Can I resume the movement timer?
Choose Resume activity or Continue on the routine timer. Review the remaining time before carrying on.
tool
I want Bounce to stay quiet during my workout.
Choose Stay quiet for the activity's company level. You can keep the illustration without spoken check-ins.
tool
I finished moving before the timer ended.
You can end the activity now. If you save a record, use what you actually did rather than the original planned duration.
tool
Will this timer continue when I lock my phone?
The browser may pause when the phone is locked. Use your device's timer for something that must work in the background.
tool
I want a timer without encouragement.
Use Timers or choose quiet company. You do not need motivational prompts to keep time.
tool
Can you log the workout just because the timer ended?
A finished timer does not prove what movement happened. Review and save the activity details yourself.
tool
I accidentally started the wrong movement timer.
End the incorrect activity, then review the right title and duration before starting again.
tool
I want to change the length of my walk.
Check the activity controls before changing the plan. Keep the saved record separate from what you originally intended.
tool

title: Return without making up for it
examples: I missed a week of movement.
Begin with what fits today. There is no exercise debt to repay before you are allowed to return.
I keep starting and stopping exercise plans.
Look for the part that repeatedly becomes difficult. A smaller or more flexible plan may be easier to return to.
I was consistent and then life got busy.
The earlier movement still happened. Adjust the next step to your current life instead of trying to recreate a different week.
I want to restart without announcing a big goal.
You can quietly choose one session. A fresh start does not need a public promise or a complete new identity.
I missed Monday so the week feels ruined.
The rest of the week is still available. Choose the next practical opportunity without making Monday decide everything.
I want a routine I can keep returning to.
Choose something manageable on an ordinary day, with an even smaller version for difficult days.
I did less this month than last month.
Look at what changed around you. A fair comparison includes time, health, responsibilities and the opportunities you actually had.
I need to restart after caring for someone.
Caring can take real energy. Begin with a small activity that fits your current responsibilities and leaves room for your own rest.
I am afraid another attempt will not last.
You do not need a lifetime promise to choose today. Make the next step useful even if the pattern changes later.
I want to celebrate coming back.
Returning is worth noticing. Keep the celebration gentle and let the next session stay manageable.

title: When movement needs tailored advice
examples: I have a heart condition; which workout is safe?
Please ask your healthcare team for exercise guidance specific to your condition. A generic routine cannot establish what is safe for you.
live
I am pregnant and want a new workout plan.
Ask your maternity team or a qualified pregnancy exercise professional about suitable activity. This recording cannot tailor a plan to your pregnancy.
live
I have just had surgery and want to exercise.
Follow your surgical team's recovery instructions and ask before adding exercise. Daywell cannot clear you to train.
live
I am returning after an injury.
Use the return-to-activity advice from your clinician or physiotherapist. Do not treat a generic app routine as rehabilitation.
live
Can you guarantee these exercises will prevent disease?
No. Movement can support wellbeing, but Daywell cannot promise disease prevention or a particular medical outcome.
live
I want to exercise to punish myself for eating.
You do not need to earn or undo food through exercise. Choose care over punishment, and seek support if this pattern is hard to interrupt.
live
I want to train through a fever.
Do not use this app to push through illness. Rest and seek medical advice if you are unwell or unsure about returning to exercise.
live
Can you design rehabilitation for my back pain?
Rehabilitation needs a qualified assessment. I can help you organise an existing professional plan, but cannot diagnose or prescribe one.
live
I feel faint and have collapsed during exercise.
Get urgent medical help now. If someone is unconscious or seriously unwell, call local emergency services; in the UK, nine nine nine.
urgent
Is this routine suitable for my child?
These routines are not a personalised children's programme. Seek age-appropriate guidance from a qualified professional rather than adapting an adult routine blindly.
live
